source.title: How Do Electrocardiogram Models Scale?
source.authors: Jia-Wei Li; Fabio Bonassi; Ming Jin; S. Gustafsson; J. Sundström; Thomas B. Schon; Antônio H. Ribeiro

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports scaling fits in ECG models, but finds they depend on architecture and pre-training paradigm, with supervised-learning saturation and varying compute-optimal allocations. It therefore refines the scope of scaling-law claims in a new modality.
record.gate_note: The study tests ECG model/data scaling, loss-to-loss transfer, and compute allocation. It does not test language models, prediction from small runs to much larger runs, or architecture details at a fixed parameter count. The fine-tuning benchmark and label-scaling results do not directly test the listed versions and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits Chinchilla-form loss laws, loss-to-loss laws and derived compute-optimal allocations for ECG models (20K–200M params, CODE data) in a new modality. It reports where the laws hold, saturate or differ by architecture, paradigm and task. This is a new-setting test bearing on V3, V5, V6 and V7, not a direct test of the language-model claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors also note Transformer-SSL overtakes ResNet-SSL only at large model sizes. They say scaling supervised labels improves ID but gives task-dependent OOD gains, and that their results explain inconsistent downstream scaling in prior ECG work.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits related joint and marginal scaling laws, but uses ECG signals, supervised and self-supervised objectives, test losses on ECG tasks, and unique training samples rather than language-model next-token loss and tokens. Training involves repeated epochs; compute-optimal allocation is derived assuming approximately stable convergence epoch counts.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes and fitted exponents vary with architecture (ResNet vs Transformer), pre-training paradigm (SL vs SSL), evaluation dataset/task, and whether evaluation is ID or OOD.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing the number of supervised pretraining labels (9 to 927, MIMIC-IV) improves ID loss, but OOD gains vary with label composition and architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling the label space in supervised pretraining improves in-distribution performance but not reliably transfer.

record.problems: The main scaling experiments use one large public pre-training dataset (CODE), two architecture families, and selected pre-training paradigms. Compute allocation depends on an approximately configuration-independent epoch-count assumption. The paper reports fit R² values, but uncertainty estimates for most scaling exponents are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-task scaling fits and best-loss entries from Figures 2 and 4, Tables S.5–S.7, and the task-by-task compute-allocation panels in Figure S.5 are not separately enumerated; the record retains the main aggregate results and explicitly described exceptions. The label-scaling and downstream fine-tuning benchmark results were left out because they do not directly test the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss is not studied; the study uses ECG models only.
No extrapolation test from small to much larger runs.
Depth and width are scaled jointly (compound scaling); shape at fixed N is not varied.
Image and video models and repeated-data comparisons are not studied. The fine-tuning transfer law in App. B.8 is not captured by any row.
No empirical compute-optimal sweep: allocation is derived analytically from Eq.(1) under a constant-epoch assumption, using downstream linear-probe loss.

missing.what: Compute-frontier fits of OOD CPSC2018 loss L*(C)=a(C+c)^-b+d: b=0.133 (Transformer-SL), 0.184 (Transformer-SSL), 0.358 (ResNet-SL); d=0.209 vs 0.184 for Transformer SL vs SSL.
Transformer-SL ID loss increases (overfits) when model size exceeds 10^7 parameters, a departure from monotone power-law scaling.
Fine-tuning transfer law D_T=k·D_F^γ1·N^γ2 for Transformer-SL: γ1 1.78–2.59 on near-domain tasks, 0.42 on EchoNext; γ2 negative everywhere.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T3: this is a new-modality test that largely reproduces power-law form, with qualifications rather than an argument that the claim is wrong. OOD linear-probe scaling rows (r9–r13) were relinked away from V5, since they measure downstream performance (V6) or only setup-dependence (V7). Fig. S.2's text extraction scrambles the β/E columns. SSL ID β values were reconstructed by matching the per-task values and means quoted in the text, so check r6/r8 against the figure. Many κ values equal exactly 0.050, suggesting a lower bound in the fitting procedure that the paper does not state. The Figure 1 benchmark of published foundation models (no clear scaling trend) is declared left out; it compares confounded models from different studies.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures ECG-model test loss, not held-out pretraining loss of language models.
No evaluation tests whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
Uses ECG samples rather than language-model tokens, and derives allocation under an approximately constant-epoch assumption; it does not test the language-model-specific split.
The study compares ResNet and Transformer families but does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Tests ECG models with supervised and self-supervised pre-training, not image or video models, repeated-data comparisons, or fine-tuning and transfer as the pre-training scaling regime.
Tests loss-to-loss relationships and linear-probe downstream test loss on ECG tasks, not language-model downstream task performance.
Shows dependence on architecture, paradigm, and dataset/task in ECG experiments; it does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, fitting methods, or language-model training schedules.

rows.subject: Transformer-SL
rows.operation_detail: Fit test loss against model parameter count.
rows.locator: Section 5; Figure 2(a); Appendix B.1, Figure S.2
rows.note: The curve is reported to bend and flatten beyond ∼106 parameters as loss approaches the estimated floor.
rows.check: The link is right. The Eq.(1) form fits (R² 0.98), but the parameter curve flattens beyond ~10^6 params under a data bottleneck. App. B.1 also says Transformer-SL ID loss worsens above 10^7 params from overfitting; the note should say so.

rows.subject: ResNet-SL

rows.locator: Section 5; Figure 2(i); Appendix B.1, Figure S.2
rows.note: The paper reports supervised-learning parameter curves flattening beyond ∼106 parameters.
rows.check: The link is right. The curve flattens beyond ~10^6 params because data is the bottleneck.

rows.locator: Section 5; Figure 2(b); Appendix B.1, Figure S.2
rows.note: The authors describe data scaling as unsaturated and dataset size as the main bottleneck for ID supervised learning.

rows.subject: ResNet-SL
rows.operation_detail: Fit test loss against pre-training dataset size.
rows.note: The authors describe the data-scaling curve as far from saturation.

rows.subject: Transformer-SSL
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate ID test loss across model parameter counts.
rows.value: No visible saturation; described as an irreducible-loss-free power law
rows.note: No numerical exponent is stated in the text for this specific marginal curve.
rows.check: A numeric value is available. Fig. S.2 joint fit gives Transformer-SSL ID α=0.464 (R² 0.957). 'Not stated' is wrong.

rows.subject: Transformer-SSL
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate ID test loss across pre-training dataset sizes.
rows.note: The paper reports that SSL models generally show unsaturated scaling across model and data sizes.
rows.check: A numeric value is available. Fig. S.2 gives Transformer-SSL ID β=0.151.

rows.subject: ResNet-SSL

rows.note: The paper reports that SSL models generally show unsaturated scaling across model and data sizes.
rows.check: A numeric value is available. Fig. S.2 gives ResNet-SSL ID β≈0.281; its OOD mean of 0.286 matches the reported 4× ResNet-SL.

rows.subject: Transformer-SL
rows.operation_detail: Fit OOD test loss against model parameter count and pre-training dataset size.
rows.measure: OOD parameter-scaling exponent α; data-scaling exponent β
rows.locator: Appendix B.1, Figure S.2 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors characterize these near-zero exponents as showing almost no OOD scaling benefit in this supervised setting.
rows.check: This is OOD linear-probe loss scaling with N and D, i.e. downstream improvement with scale (V6), not pretraining loss (V5). The authors call it 'almost no OOD benefit', so the state is absent, not partial.

rows.subject: ResNet and Transformer models
rows.operation_detail: Compare mean OOD parameter-scaling exponents across architecture families.
rows.measure: Relative parameter-scaling efficiency by mean exponent α
rows.value: ResNet models have 1.3× larger mean α
rows.note: The paper also states a 10-fold parameter increase in ResNet corresponds to a 19-fold increase in Transformer parameters for matching excess-loss reduction.
rows.check: This is a ratio of mean OOD exponents across architectures and shows only setup-dependence, not V5. It checks against Fig. S.2 means: 0.442/0.348≈1.3.

rows.subject: ResNet and Transformer models
rows.operation_detail: Compare mean OOD parameter-scaling exponents across architecture families.
rows.measure: Relative parameter-scaling efficiency by mean exponent α
rows.value: ResNet models have 2.5× larger mean α
rows.note: The paper also states a 10-fold parameter increase in ResNet corresponds to a 288-fold increase in Transformer parameters for matching excess-loss reduction.
rows.check: This is a ratio comparison and bears only on V7. It checks: 0.529/0.214≈2.5.

rows.subject: Transformer models
rows.operation_detail: Compare mean OOD data-scaling exponents across pre-training paradigms.
rows.measure: Relative data-scaling efficiency by mean exponent β
rows.note: The authors report the paradigm gap as favoring SSL.
rows.check: This is a ratio comparison and bears only on V7. It checks: 0.313/0.019≈16.

rows.subject: ResNet models
rows.operation_detail: Compare mean OOD data-scaling exponents across pre-training paradigms.
rows.measure: Relative data-scaling efficiency by mean exponent β
rows.note: The authors report SSL as more data-efficient for OOD performance.
rows.check: This is a ratio comparison and bears only on V7. It checks: 0.286/0.071≈4.

rows.subject: Transformer-SL
rows.operation_detail: Derive and plot the compute-optimal parameter allocation from fitted loss scaling.
rows.measure: Exponent in compute-optimal parameter count N*(C)
rows.note: The accompanying text says 90% of marginal compute is directed to data.
rows.check: N*∝C^{β/(α+β)} is derived analytically from fitted Eq.(1) on OOD linear-probe loss, under an assumed constant epoch count. The power form is assumed, not measured from compute sweeps. Per Fig. S.5, the exponent varies by task (0.03–0.27 for Transformer-SL).

source_check.correct: N* ∝ C^0.10 is an analytical allocation derived from fitted OOD loss under a constant-epoch assumption. State: observed for V7 setup dependence; cannot_determine for an independently tested V3 allocation law.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 5(b), caption; Appendix B.4, Eqs. S.3–S.7.
source_check.problem: The partial state conflates setup-dependent fitted allocations with evidence that stable compute-optimal scaling holds incompletely.

rows.subject: Transformer-SL
rows.operation_detail: Fit OOD loss as a power law of excess ID test loss.
rows.note: The reported mean κ is below 1; the paper says κ<1 indicates a transfer bottleneck.
rows.check: The loss-to-loss power-law fits are decent (mean R² 0.83), but coupling is weak (κ=0.128). Several per-task κ sit at exactly 0.050, which looks like a fitting lower bound.

rows.subject: ResNet-SL
rows.operation_detail: Fit OOD loss as a power law of excess ID test loss.
rows.note: The reported mean κ is below 1; the paper says κ<1 indicates a transfer bottleneck.
rows.check: Same as r18: weak coupling, with κ=0.050 on EchoNext, ICU and sex, apparently at the bound.

rows.subject: Transformer-SSL
rows.operation_detail: Fit OOD loss as a power law of excess ID test loss.
rows.note: The reported mean κ is below 1, and varies substantially by OOD task.
rows.check: κ<1 means diminishing returns, not unpredictability. The fits are predictive (mean R² 0.85), so observed, not partial. ICU κ is at the 0.050 bound.

rows.subject: ResNet-SSL
rows.operation_detail: Fit OOD loss as a power law of excess ID test loss.
rows.note: The reported mean κ is below 1, and varies substantially by OOD task.
rows.check: Predictable fits (mean R² 0.83); κ<1 alone is not a shortfall against V6.

rows.subject: Transformer-SSL
rows.operation_detail: Fit OOD loss as a power law of excess ID test loss.
rows.note: Higher transfer efficiency than Transformer-SL, but κ remains below 1.
rows.check: Transformer-SSL EchoNext κ=0.339 with R² 0.86. The Transformer-SL baseline of 0.050 is likely at the fit bound.

rows.subject: ResNet-SSL
rows.operation_detail: Fit OOD loss as a power law of excess ID test loss.
rows.measure: Transfer exponent κ relative to ResNet-SL
rows.note: The paper describes this as the largest ResNet transfer-efficiency advantage; κ remains below 1.
rows.check: ResNet-SSL sex κ=0.383 (R² 0.94) vs ResNet-SL 0.050 (bound), giving ≈7.6×. The value could be given as κ=0.383.
